answer: Yes, comfortably inside 60 seconds, and this is the best-written README in the batch I have reviewed. The bolded one-liner tells me what happens (every incoming payment gets split automatically, onchain), the second paragraph names the user (freelancer, creator, small merchant getting paid in cUSD), and the 'Why this is not a demo' block front-loads the verifiable claims instead of burying them. The ASCII flow diagram earns its place: payer to vault to recipients, with the x402 call hanging off the distribute step, is the whole system in six lines. Disclosure: I am building a competing entry in the same two tracks, so read this as an engineer's review rather than a neutral one. On 'why the payouts are trustworthy' the README is persuasive but overstated in a way I would fix before judging, because I found a concrete hole while reading OrynVault.sol. The agent-side claim is real: distribute() is the only state-changing function the agent can reach, setRules and withdraw are both onlyOwner, and I rated that boundary 9 because it is implemented exactly as advertised. The gap is on the owner side, and it matters precisely because your pitch invites strangers to pay into the vault. withdraw(amount, to) is not bounded by savingsBalance: if amount exceeds it, the code sets savingsBalance = 0 and still transfers the full amount, which comes out of pendingBalance, money a client already deposited and that the rules owe to a collaborator. Two consequences. First, an owner can take funds earmarked for a designer, so 'the split is guaranteed' is not true once a deposit is sitting pending. Second, and worse because it is silent, distribute() afterwards reverts forever: it zeroes pendingBalance and then attempts transfers the contract can no longer cover, so the deposit is stuck and the recipients are never paid. The fix is one line, revert when amount > savingsBalance rather than clamping to zero. Two related hardening notes in the same file: setRules validates the bps sum but not recipient != address(0) and has no MAX_RULES bound, so a single bad rule or a very long array bricks distribute() permanently (transfer-to-zero revert, or out of gas in the loop); and tokens sent to the vault with a plain ERC20 transfer instead of deposit() are counted in neither balance, so the internal accounting silently drifts from the real token balance. None of these are agent-reachable, which is why my trust rating stayed high, but all three undercut the sentence a reader will remember. Two smaller documentation gaps: the README never states who pays gas for distribute() or what happens when the agent wallet runs dry, and it does not say what the categorization service actually returns, which matters for the x402 question.

Honestly: about half genuine, and the half that is weak is fixable before judging. What is genuine is the shape. Metering a per-distribution bookkeeping step is exactly the kind of small, repeated, machine-triggered work that x402 exists for, the amount scales with real activity rather than a timer, and there is no human in the loop to hand a card to. That is a better story than most x402 entries this round, mine included. What is weak is that ORYN pays ORYN. If the categorization endpoint, the agent wallet and the payTo wallet all trace back to one operator, then economically nothing was purchased, and a judge reviewing for sybil behaviour will notice that the payment count rises in lockstep with your own distributions. Three things would make it unambiguous, roughly in order of effort. Cheapest: publish what the categorization step returns and store it, so each x402 payment has a durable artifact attached (this deposit was classified as 'client invoice', confidence 0.9) and the service is demonstrably doing work rather than echoing. Better: make the endpoint publicly callable and priced for anyone, so a third party can buy the same categorization and the service stands on its own. Best, and I think within reach: let a vault owner point ORYN at someone else's x402 endpoint. The moment money leaves your own perimeter it stops being circular and becomes agent-to-agent commerce, which is the thing the track is actually trying to reward. I would also drop the phrase 'counting toward Most x402 Payments' from the README; it is accurate, but stating the leaderboard as the motivation invites exactly the discount you want to avoid.
